name: English (New York City)
variety: New York City English: the traditional accent of the city and its near suburbs as described by Labov (1966), with the changes now under way noted
sources: Labov, William (2006). The Social Stratification of English in New York City. 2nd edition. Cambridge University Press. (First edition 1966.)
Labov, William; Ash, Sharon; Boberg, Charles (2006). The Atlas of North American English: Phonetics, Phonology and Sound Change. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Wells, J. C. (1982). Accents of English. Volume 3: Beyond the British Isles. Cambridge University Press.
Gordon, Matthew J. (2004). New York, Philadelphia, and other northern cities: phonology. In Schneider et al. (eds.), A Handbook of Varieties of English, volume 1. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.
Newman, Michael (2014). New York City English. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton.
Becker, Kara (2014). (r) we there yet? The change to rhoticity in New York City English. Language Variation and Change 26(2), 141-168.
Becker, Kara and Wong, Amy Wing-mei (2010). The short-a system of New York City English: an update. University of Pennsylvania Working Papers in Linguistics 15(2).
Lisker, Leigh and Abramson, Arthur S. (1964). A cross-language study of voicing in initial stops: acoustical measurements. Word 20(3), 384-422.
contrasts: short-a split: tense /eə/ (bad, man, pass, cab) versus lax /æ/ (bat, back, pal), a phonemic split because some words are exceptions to the conditioning (tense avenue, lax auxiliary can against tense noun can)
LOT versus THOUGHT: the two are kept far apart, THOUGHT being raised to [ɔə], [oə] or [ʊə] (cot versus caught, Don versus dawn)
traditionally non-rhotic, with centring diphthongs in NEAR, SQUARE, START, NORTH and CURE; /r/ after a vowel is variable and increasing
Mary, marry and merry are three different vowels, and hurry [ʌ] differs from furry [ɝ]
orange, horrible, Florida have the vowel of LOT plus /r/, not that of NORTH
FOOT versus STRUT, as in all North American accents; no TRAP-BATH split of the British kind, BATH words follow the short-a split
in non-rhotic speech NORTH, FORCE and THOUGHT are one vowel (source = sauce)
older speakers keep PALM (father, balm) apart from LOT (bother, bomb)
allophony: short-a is tense before the voiced stops /b d ɡ/, /dʒ/, the voiceless fricatives /f θ s ʃ/ and the nasals /m n/ when that consonant closes the syllable (cab, bad, bag, badge, half, bath, pass, cash, ham, man); it is lax before voiceless stops, /ŋ/, /l/, /v z/ and in open syllables (planet, hammer); stems keep their vowel before a suffix (passing, manning tense); function words are lax (can, am, and, had); younger speakers are moving towards tensing before nasals only
tense short-a is an ingliding vowel that ranges from [ɛə] to [ɪə]; the raised forms are stigmatised and are lowered in careful speech
THOUGHT and CLOTH (coffee, off, dog, talk) are raised and ingliding; raised forms are also corrected in careful speech
/r/ after a vowel is variably dropped, more in casual speech and lower social groups; NURSE is now rhotic [ɝ] for nearly all speakers; an intrusive /r/ occurs (law and order, idea of)
the old NURSE form [əɪ] before a consonant (bird, third, work) is nearly extinct; it never occurred at the end of a word (fur)
/θ ð/ are often dental stops or affricates [t̪ d̪] (these, those, three) in casual speech
/t d n l/ are dental or laminal for many speakers
/t/ between vowels is a tap; /t/ before syllabic /l/ or /n/ may be a glottal stop (bottle, button)
/l/ is dark, also at the start of a syllable, and may be vocalised after a vowel
PRICE has a back start [ɑɪ] and MOUTH a front start [æʊ]
GOAT and GOOSE stay back; after coronal consonants GOOSE has a front onglide
ng may be [ŋɡ] before a vowel for some speakers (Long Island)
phonotactics: in non-rhotic speech /r/ occurs only before a vowel, with linking and intrusive /r/
lax vowels need a following consonant in a stressed syllable
/ŋ/ does not begin a syllable; /h/ only begins a syllable and does not precede /j/

stress.rule: As in other accents of American English: fixed for each word, with Germanic initial stress and weight-sensitive Latinate stress.
stress.cues: pitch movement on accented syllables, duration, loudness and vowel quality

rhythm.vowel_reduction: strong: unstressed syllables have schwa, [ɪ] or a syllabic consonant
rhythm.notes: I know of no nPVI value for New York City English.

length.notes: Length is not contrastive by itself; tense and lax short-a differ in quality, gliding and length together. Vowels are shorter before voiceless consonants.

voice_onset_time_ms.source: Lisker and Abramson 1964: American English speakers, isolated words; not specific to New York City. Values for /b d g/ are those of the short-lag tokens; some speakers prevoice.

intonation.declarative: high accents on stressed syllables, falling nuclear accent and low boundary (H* L-L%)
intonation.yes_no_question: low accent followed by a rise to a high boundary (L* H-H%)
intonation.wh_question: falling nuclear accent and low boundary
intonation.continuation: fall followed by a slight rise (L-H%) or a level high end
intonation.accent_shape: H* peak on the accented syllable; L+H* for contrast
intonation.notes: The general pattern of American English; I know of no instrumental study that sets New York City intonation apart.

phonation: glottal replacement of /t/ before syllabic consonants

problems: NURSE is always the diphthong [əɪ], also at the end of a word and before a vowel (fur [fəɪ], hurry [həɪɹi], girl, work): this form is nearly extinct, it occurred only before a consonant, and hurry has [ʌ] in this accent

LOT uses the rounded British vowel (phoneme 0 with formant file vowel/0: lot, cot, bother come out as [ɒ]), where New York has an unrounded [ɑ]; dog and chocolate get the same vowel instead of the raised THOUGHT vowel

short-a tensing has no lexical or grammatical exceptions: the function words can, and, am, had are tense, stems before a suffix are lax (passing, manning), and badge is lax because /dʒ/ is not in the list of tensing consonants
the voice is fully non-rhotic and has no intrusive /r/ (law and order, the idea is); present-day speakers are variably rhotic
/θ ð/ are always fricatives, and there is no glottal stop in bottle or button
the tunes are the default English ones, and wh-questions get the rising question tune
good: the short-a split: a raised ingliding vowel [ɛə] before voiced stops, nasals and voiceless fricatives in closed syllables, lax [æ] elsewhere and in open syllables (cab, bad, ham against cap, back, planet)
THOUGHT and CLOTH have a raised ingliding vowel (coffee, off, lost, talk)
Mary, marry and merry are three vowels, and orange, horrible, tomorrow have [ɑ]
non-rhotic long vowels and centring diphthongs; /t/ is tapped between vowels; /d/ is dental; /h/ is dropped before /j/

notes: New York City English is changing: rhoticity is rising, the short-a split is giving way to a nasal system among younger speakers, and THOUGHT is lowering (Becker 2014; Becker and Wong 2010). The profile describes the traditional system that the eSpeak NG voice aims at. In the diphthong list /eə/ is tense short-a, /ɔə/ is THOUGHT, and ɑə, ɪə, ɛə, ʊə are the non-rhotic forms of START, NEAR, SQUARE, CURE. I give no formant values: the Atlas of North American English has them, and I cannot quote them with confidence.
